title: What defines each jazz style: Bird's influence and others following
summary: Ridley asks whether period styles define jazz; Sam says a unique voice like Bird's draws everyone in, and compares it to disco.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Let me back up a second and ask you something. Now, you mentioned, like, about bebop and how that was a word, and like you said, much like Dizzy Gillespie--

--and going into the scat singing kind of thing--would you agree that in talking about jazz and just looking at the various periods, what it, how the music evolved would you agree that in each of those periods that there seemed to be, like--OK, take into like we mentioned, Louis Armstrong that there were certain techniques that he utilizes, the way he approached improvisation that sort of outlined himself as an individual--artist and that sort of sets the guidelines or parameters, you know, like from which the Louis Armstrong style, or the New Orleans style and those guys coming through that particular type of music sort of played off of that kind of thing. Would you agree that it's, that there are certain kinds of, you know,

like, approaches to harmony, approaches to melody and approaches to rhythm that seem to be, um, a part of each of those particular years. Like you mentioned the swing years, certain way that Lester Young approached the melody, certain way...Hawkins approached melody, certain way Dizzy Gillespie or Miles or Charlie Parker---- in terms of what identifies their style, would you say that is what makes the difference within the music? Can that be used to in terms of defining what jazz is about?

It could be, and it could, and then again I-I'm not, see, see like uh, like I said in the (inaudible) a variety of style of music. Uh, like we had the blues when I was a kid coming up. OK, and you had, you--then you had the uh, you had your country and westerns, you know, that's a strong music--country and western--don't let nobody, uh, kid you about that.
You know I don't, I'm from Indiana.

Yeah. And uh, you had your blues singers. We had a variety of blues singers. Then you had your, your commercial type music. It's it's all going on the same thing the same way today, man. It's there's no change. OK, uh, when--I understand that when Louis Armstrong was a, was a, young man uh, I think he was an orphan...
Well, he was put in an orphanage.

So, uh, he uh, in those, in those schools, man, you know, they taught you well, you know. They taught you well and they had good teachers in there which they talked--those guys were very technical on the instruments. And, so, each man had a mind of his own, man, you know, and so if a guy come up with an idea we freeze or we go on. And we sit down and think of a melody and make up a--it's all in making up a song it's like you go home and you compose, and you go home and compose a say Larry, that's your--that's Larry Ridley, man, that's all yours. Now it's up to the rest of the world to uh, uh, when they hear your melody, man, it's up to the world to, for, for them to, to like it or dislike it if they want to, you know. OK, so, you might come up with a style, you know, that, which every-body likes. You know, just like when Bird came on the scene man, there were great musicians on the scene before Bird came. So when Bird came on the scene, scene with his unique style of playing, then everybody say "wow" man, this guy here, this guy here plays different from everybody, you know. Then everybody's, you know, start falling in, you know, trying trying to, trying to emulate this man, trying to--you understand what I mean? Trying to, uh, uh, learn his ideas and his technique and his his ways of thinking, you know. Trying to handle

this man. So now this man is almost like a leader, you see. OK, when he brought that stuff up here to New York, from Kansas City, you see, who knows how long he been doing it down there in Kansas City. The man that taught him. how bad was he? You know? But he's, Charlie Parker swears by the man who taught him, you see. See, he was the greatest man he ever heard, see. The man got to be the uh, uh, uh, a great man, he taught him what he knew, you see. So he came up with this new idea so they brought this stuff up here, so everybody heard this unique way of playing and everybody joined in. So you find another--here's another guy that's playing the trumpet, you know, playing like Roy Eldridge, he joined in. He changed his whole conception of playing to uh, uh, uh, like Bird, you see. So these guys get together man, and and and now this new music is is formed, man, you see. Everybody follows, man, it it it's a funny thing I hear man, it's a, when one person starts something everybody join in and get in line and try and follow. And when this, so called, disco stuff--it's the hardest thing in the world, man, it's all over the world, man, you know. And it ain't nothing but a dude playing--it's nothing but a back beat--that's all it is man. A back beat going on so that gives you the rhythm that always support the rhythm that back beat.
